plan.why: Rising story with low creator competition. Women 45+ are a core audience, and the honest twist that the headline benefit is mostly semaglutide fits our calm format, which wins on Instagram and YouTube. | fact-check: Verified on Healio, Oct 23, 2026. Retrospective observational cohort, Mayo Clinic, presented by Regina Castaneda, MD at The Menopause Society meeting. 2,379 women aged 45+ with BMI ≥27 on semaglutide or tirzepatide. At 1 year: 11% vs 9.5% (P=.001). Healio says the significant differences were with semaglutide. For tirzepatide it reports only a 'similar directional effect' at early timepoints that 'did not reach statistical significance'. The angle's 'modest at 3 months and not significant after that' implies a significant 3-month result, and the source doesn't support that. Fix it. Other outlets (HealthDay/US News) give a different total (~3,900 women), so cite Healio's 2,379 only and don't mix in other figures. Note: an earlier, separate Mayo analysis (2025, 120 women on tirzepatide, 19.2% vs 14.0%) is what drove the 'hormone therapy boosts tirzepatide' headlines. If it's mentioned, label it as a separate, smaller observational study. Must say: hormone therapy isn't a weight-loss treatment (the researchers stressed this), and it's a separate decision with a clinician. Never suggest starting or stopping it. Title: drop 'HRT' (abbreviation) or keep it as the only abbreviation. Consider 'Tirzepatide in Menopause: Does Hormone Therapy Add More?'

factcheck.summary:
I checked every claim against the Healio (Oct 23, 2026) and Patient Care (Oct 22, 2026) reports on the Mayo Clinic abstract from The Menopause Society 2026 meeting (Oct 20–24, San Diego), plus the joint nutrition advisory and MedlinePlus. The core facts are correct:
- Women 45 and older with BMI 27 or higher.
- 2,379 women in the semaglutide cohort.
- 11.0% vs 9.5% weight loss at 12 months (P=.001).
- The tirzepatide cohort (1,476 women) was analysed separately. It showed a small gap at 3 months (6.6% vs 5.9%) that was no longer significant from 12 months on.
- The study was a retrospective, observational, propensity-matched EHR cohort presented as conference data.
- The lead researcher's point that weight management is not an indication for hormone therapy is reported.
- Protein plus strength training comes from the advisory, and nausea and constipation are on the tirzepatide label.

The framing is right: "linked to", "on average", observational, not peer-reviewed, no claim to cause. The safety lines are all there: the kidney caveat, "don't stop or change", "Not personal advice" and the prescriber line. The script is about 150 words.

Note that Healio wrongly says 2,379 was the total for both drugs. The script uses Patient Care's breakdown, which is correct.

Four minor precision fixes are listed below. None of them is a reason to hold or revise.

issues.claim: Eleven percent. Versus nine point five percent.
issues.problem: The measure isn't named. Viewers can't tell it is the % of body weight lost, and the sizes of the two groups (793 on hormone therapy vs 1,586 without) are missing. The craft rules say every spoken number needs its measure and its group sizes.
issues.fix: Narration: "Among two thousand three hundred seventy-nine on semaglutide, those on hormone therapy lost a bit more body weight at one year, on average. Eleven percent. Versus nine point five percent." stat_label: "Semaglutide: % body weight lost, hormone therapy (793) vs none (1,586), 1 yr, on average"

issues.claim: in a separate group of women on tirzepatide, the gap was smaller and less consistent
issues.problem: This is accurate but vague. The source shows a small gap at 3 months (6.6% vs 5.9%) that was not significant from 12 months onward. Saying exactly that is more precise and pays off the twist better.
issues.fix: Narration: "The twist: in a separate group of about fifteen hundred women on tirzepatide, there was a small early gap, but by one year it wasn't significant." On-screen/list item: "Tirzepatide (separate group, 1,476): small early gap, not significant at 1 yr"

issues.claim: The lead researcher says weight loss isn't a reason for hormone therapy.
issues.problem: This paraphrases Dr. Castaneda's quoted words, "Weight management is not an indication for hormone therapy." It isn't wrong, but it's closer to the source to name her and keep her wording.
issues.fix: Narration: "The lead researcher, Dr. Regina Castaneda, says weight management is not a reason to start hormone therapy. That's a separate choice to make with your clinician." List item: "Weight management isn't a reason for hormone therapy"

issues.problem: The headlines hedge ("may equal greater", "linked to"). Saying they flatly "say yes" slightly overstates them.
issues.fix: "Does hormone therapy boost tirzepatide in menopause? Some headlines suggest it."

audio.soundNotes: Thinned redundant simultaneous SFX layers (swell/whip, swoosh/whoosh, pop/tick pairs and the triple-blip cluster near 35–36s) to keep stacking at 1–2 effects per moment; pulled down a few cues that measured louder than the voice (swoosh at 5.8s and 20.3s, the pop at 52.3s) into the −14/−20 dB speech window, and lightly boosted the lone pause-cue at 22.1s toward the −6/−12 dB pause target. Eased and simplified the cluster of transition cues around the two safety/caution lines (60s and 64.5s) so the serious messaging isn't crowded by sound. Music under voice is already on target (−13.5 dB) so gain stays at 1.0; pause-level music (−19.1 dB) runs quieter than ideal but can't be fixed with a single multiplier without overshooting speech levels, so it's addressed in the music brief's dynamic arc instead. Added 4 subtle custom accents for the first stat reveal, the "not significant" letdown, the "protect muscle" tip, and the stop/start safety line.
